scenes.heading: Naming organic compounds
scenes.sub: Read a name, draw the molecule
scenes.say: Every organic compound has a systematic name that tells you exactly how its atoms are joined, so anyone in the world can draw the same molecule from the name alone.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: A street address: street name, house number, type of building
scenes.science: IUPAC name: chain length, position number, functional group ending
scenes.breaks: streets are fixed, but the parent chain is the longest chain holding the functional group, and it may bend.
scenes.say: An IUPAC name is like a street address. The prefix, like prop or but, is the street, telling you how many carbons. The numbers are house numbers showing where things sit. And the ending, such as ol for an alcohol, tells you what lives there.
scenes.caption: An IUPAC name is like a street address. The prefix, like prop- or but-, is the street, telling you how many carbons. The numbers are house numbers showing where things sit. And the ending, such as -ol for an alcohol, tells you what lives there.

scenes.heading: Chain length prefixes
scenes.say: For chain length, remember monkeys eat peeled bananas: meth, eth, prop, but, for one to four carbons. Then pentagon, hexagon, heptagon and octopus give five to eight.

scenes.heading: Name it in four moves
steps: Find the longest chain with the group
Give the group the lowest number
scenes.say: Name it in four moves. Find the longest chain holding the functional group; it may bend. Number from the end that gives the group the lowest number. Add branches in alphabetical order. Then add the ending.

scenes.heading: Endings
scenes.say: Each family has its own ending. Aldehydes, carboxylic acids and amides are always on carbon one, so they don't need a number, and their carbon counts in the chain. So C H three C H two C O O H is propanoic acid, not ethanoic acid.
scenes.caption: Each family has its own ending. Aldehydes, carboxylic acids and amides are always on C1, so they don't need a number, and their carbon counts in the chain. So CH₃CH₂COOH is propanoic acid, not ethanoic acid.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Name CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂OH.
lines: Longest chain with the –OH: 4 C → but-
Number from the –OH end: –OH on C1
scenes.say: The longest chain holding the O H has four carbons, so the stem is but. Number from the O H end, so it's on carbon one, and the methyl branch lands on carbon three. That's three-methylbutan-one-ol, a primary alcohol.
scenes.caption: The longest chain holding the –OH has four carbons, so the stem is but-. Number from the –OH end, so it's on C1, and the methyl branch lands on C3. That's 3-methylbutan-1-ol, a primary alcohol.

scenes.heading: Esters: alcohol says hi first
points: Formula often shows the acid part first
scenes.say: Esters have two-word names, and the alcohol says hi first. The alcohol part ends in yl, and the acid part ends in oate. So the ester from ethanoic acid and ethanol is ethyl ethanoate, even though its formula shows the acid part first.
scenes.caption: Esters have two-word names, and the alcohol says hi first. The alcohol part ends in -yl, and the acid part ends in -oate. So the ester from ethanoic acid and ethanol is ethyl ethanoate, even though its formula shows the acid part first.

points: Lowest number for the functional group
scenes.say: Quick recap. Find the longest chain, give the functional group the lowest number, add branches alphabetically, then the ending. For esters, the alcohol part comes first. Now try the practice questions!
